questionStem: A//-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of headache, confusion, and blurred vision. He has not had any recent trauma to the head or eyes. He has chronic hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, irritable bowel syndrome, and bilateral hearing loss. Current medications are hydrochlorothiazide, glipizide, amlodipine, losartan, and chlordiazepoxide. On arrival, he is holding his head in his hands. He is oriented to name and place but not to date of birth, month, year, or the current president. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 64/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 230/130 mm Hg. Visual acuity is 20/30 in both eyes. Visual fields are full. Funduscopic examination shows blurred optic disc margins and several slit-like hemorrhages in both fundi. ACT scan of the head shows a hypoattenuated area in both occipital lobes and an old lacunar infarct in the basal ganglia and thalami. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: Hypertensive encephalopathy results from acute and/or severe increases in blood pressure. It potentially manifests with headache, vomiting, agitation, altered mental status, and seizure, and may progress to obtundation and coma. Visual symptoms may result from cortical dysfunction or from hypertensive retinopathy, including retinal hemorrhages and exudates. Treatment includes carefully lowering the blood pressure while avoiding excessively rapid drops in blood pressure, which can cause end-organ ischemia. In general, a decrease in the mean arterial pressure of 25% within the first hour is appropriate, with gradual correction over the next day or more following. Intravenous agents such as labetalol, esmolol, nicardipine, and nitroprusside are preferred for initial management.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Oral 81-mg aspirin (Choice A) can be used as secondary prevention of ischemic stroke. While this patient does have evidence of prior strokes on CT scan, his acute encephalopathy is secondary to his increased blood pressure, and primary management should be focused on lowering his blood pressure. Intravenous alteplase (Choice B) is a fibrinolytic medication used for ischemic strokes that binds to fibrin clots and converts plasminogen to plasmin, which lyses clots. If given early (generally within 3 to 4.5 hours), alteplase may promote neurologic recovery. This patient has evidence of prior strokes on CT scan, likely secondary to his uncontrolled hypertension, but is well outside of the window for receiving alteplase. Additionally, blood pressure greater than 180/110 mm Hg is a contraindication to receiving alteplase as there is increased risk for hemorrhagic conversion. Intravenous dexamethasone (Choice C) is sometimes used in cases of spinal cord compression or cerebral edema secondary to brain tumors. Corticosteroids are not a part of the management of hypertensive encephalopathy. Intravenous heparin (Choice D) may be indicated in the event of a thromboembolic ischemic stroke caused by underlying atrial fibrillation. This patient has no evidence of an underlying cardiac arrhythmia, and his strokes are likely caused by his underlying poorly controlled hypertension. Educational Objective: Hypertensive encephalopathy results from acute and/or severe increases in blood pressure. questionStem: A5/-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after he was found walking unsteadily and speaking in a confused and incoherent manner. Neurologic examination shows bilateral abducens nerve palsies, coarse nystagmus in all directions of gaze, and severe truncal ataxia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Vitamin B,, or thiamine, plays a complex role in neuronal physiology including in axon conduction, glucose utilization, and neurotransmitter synthesis. Thiamine deficiency results in neuronal damage through a mechanism that likely involves oxidative toxicity. Thiamine deficiency causes two potential syndromes: Wernicke encephalopathy and Korsakoff syndrome. The classic triad of Wernicke encephalopathy demonstrates encephalopathy, ataxia, and oculomotor dysfunction caused by neuronal damage in the cerebellum, midbrain, and pons. Common ocular manifestations include nystagmus and horizontal gaze palsy as a result of damage to the abducens nuclei. Thiamine deficiency is most encountered in the setting of alcohol use disorder due to poor nutritional intake, thiamine malabsorption, and impaired cellular utilization of thiamine. Over time, thiamine deficiency can result in damage and atrophy of the mammillary bodies, visible on MRI of the brain, which manifests as Wernicke encephalopathy. The symptoms of Wernicke encephalopathy are reversible but increase the risk for developing Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome in chronic alcohol users if not immediately treated with high-dose parenteral thiamine. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is an irreversible condition that features psychosis, anterograde and retrograde amnesia, and the consequent tendency to confabulate, or verbalize false stories or memories to compensate for the inability to remember.

Huntington disease (Choice B) is a hereditary, progressive neurodegenerative disorder associated with atrophy of the caudate nuclei in the basal ganglia. The disease usually presents with an insidious onset of psychiatric and cognitive symptoms, followed by motor symptoms (eg, chorea, hypotonia, dystonia, loss of voluntary control of movements). Lead encephalopathy (Choice C) presents with cognitive dysfunction, encephalopathy, hearing loss, and peripheral neuropathy. Distal motor neuropathy causes lower motor neuron signs, including weakness, atrophy, hypotonia, and hyporeflexia. Non-neurologic manifestations of lead poisoning include renal tubular dysfunction, vomiting, abdominal pain, constipation, and anemia. Multiple sclerosis (Choice D) is an autoimmune demyelinating disease that presents with focal neurologic deficits separated in space and time. questionStem: A24-year-old man comes to the physician 1 day after he had a generalized tonic-clonic seizure at work. His symptoms began with a rising sensation in the upper middle abdomen. His coworker told him that he started to stare, licked his lips, and then fell to the floor. He had generalized shaking of his arms and legs. After he awakened, he was confused for several minutes and smelled an odor of burnt rubber that his coworkers did not notice. He has noticed a similar odor three times in the past 2 months. He was hit by a baseball bat at the age of 12 years and had a brief loss of consciousness. He has been otherwise healthy. Physical and neurologic examinations show no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely location of the abnormality?
correctExplanation: Focal-onset impaired awareness seizures are also called complex partial seizures. As this name suggests, these seizures affect a specific (focal) region of the brain and therefore produce motor or sensory symptoms that are localized to one or a few areas of the body. Patients will be unresponsive during the seizure (impaired awareness). Focal seizures can spread to the bilateral hemispheres, evolving into generalized tonic-clonic seizures, as in this patient. Tonic-clonic seizures are characterized by the sudden onset of muscle contractions followed by rhythmic jerking of the extremities. Oral automatisms and autonomic disturbances such as an epigastric rising sensation, as in this patient, are suggestive of a temporal lobe lesion, the most common origin of seizures. Manual automatisms and upper limb dystonia can also occur in temporal lobe seizures. Patients may experience visual, auditory, or sensory auras preceding the seizure. Focal-onset impaired awareness seizures are often accompanied by a brief postictal state marked by confusion and fatigue. These seizures will demonstrate localized rhythmic activity with generalized slowing on EEG. Treatment requires antiepileptic medication. For patients with refractory temporal lobe epilepsy, surgical excision of the lesion can be considered.

Cerebellar involvement more typically occurs in the setting of generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Frontal lobe (Choice C) lesions can also present with focal seizures with impaired awareness. Disturbance of the higher cognitive functions of the frontal lobe can lead to features such as speech disturbances, complex automatisms, and strong emotional expressions such as crying or laughing. Focal seizures with intact awareness with motor symptoms may also occur as a result of involvement of the primary motor cortex. Parietal lobe (Choice E) lesions can result in focal seizure activity involving the primary somatosensory cortex, resulting in sensory disturbances such as numbness, tingling, warmth, or pain. questionStem: A6/-year-old man has had four acute episodes of aphasia over the past year. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 84/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 142/82 mm Hg. Serum studies show a glucose concentration of 150 mg/dL, total cholesterol concentration of 296 mg/dL, and HDL-cholesterol concentration of 28 mg/dL. Carotid ultrasonography shows 90% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery. Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy to decrease this patient's risk for a stroke?

choices.A: Control of blood pressure with diet and medication
choices.B: Control of serum LDL-cholesterol concentration with diet and medication
choices.C: Control of serum glucose concentration with diet, oral agents, or insulin
choices.D: Control of ventricular rate with digoxin

correctExplanation: This patient with four separate episodes of acute aphasia that self-resolved has a presentation concerning for multiple transient ischemic attacks (TIAs). TIA is defined as a transient episode of neurologic dysfunction caused by focal brain, spinal cord, or retinal ischemia without evidence of infarction. The symptoms last less than 24 hours by definition and may last as little as a few minutes. Patients with TIAs are at increased risk for having an ischemic stroke; therefore, management of patients with a TIA should focus on identification and treatment of modifiable risk factors. Such risk factors include large vessel atherosclerosis, arrhythmias, known cardiac thrombus, smoking, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and hypercoagulable states. Patients who have been diagnosed with TIA should undergo MRI, Doppler ultrasonography of the carotid arteries, echocardiography, and cardiac monitoring. Patients with 70% to 99% stenosis of the carotid arteries should undergo carotid endarterectomy or carotid stenting to decrease their subsequent risk for stroke.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Control of blood pressure and control of serum LDL-cholesterol concentration with diet and medication (Choices A and B) and control of serum glucose concentration with diet, oral agents, or insulin (Choice C) are all important measures that should be taken to decrease the risk for stroke in this patient. Aspirin therapy (Choice E) is also indicated as secondary stroke prevention in this patient. However, carotid endarterectomy should take precedence for this patient with known significant carotid artery atherosclerosis, as this was likely the direct embolic source for his ischemic event and would lead to the greatest reduction in risk for subsequent stroke. Control of ventricular rate with digoxin (Choice D) would not be appropriate for this patient with a normal heart rate. Digoxin may be used to achieve rate control in patients with atrial fibrillation who do not have an adequate response to more conventional therapies such as beta blockers and calcium channel blockers. While atrial fibrillation is a known risk factor for thromboembolic strokes, controlling the heart rate does not decrease that risk. Therefore, patients with atrial fibrillation and increased stroke risk should be on warfarin therapy (Choice F) or another anticoagulant medication such as rivaroxaban or dabigatran. Educational Objective: Transient ischemic attack (TIA) is defined as a transient episode of neurologic dysfunction caused by focal brain, spinal cord, or retinal ischemia without evidence of infarction. questionStem: A60-year-old woman is brought to the office by her husband because of a 6-week history of progressive unsteadiness, incoordination, and slurred speech. During the past 6 months, she also has had a nonproductive cough, fatigue, and a 7-kg (15-Ib) unintentional weight loss despite no change in appetite. She has not seen a physician in more than 10 years and does not take any medications. She has smoked fifteen cigarettes daily for the past 40 years. She drinks alcoholic beverages only on social occasions. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 70/min, respirations are 13/min, and blood pressure is 130/85 mm Hg. Physical examination shows dysarthria, but no aphasia is noted. Cranial nerves are intact except for bilateral horizontal nystagmus. She has no focal muscle weakness or sensory deficit. Finger-nose testing and heel-shin testing discloses bilateral dysmetria. Deep tendon reflexes are 2+. The patient is unable to tandem walk. MRI of the brain discloses multiple T-2 hyperintensities in both cerebral hemispheres and mild cerebellar atrophy with enhancement of the cerebellar folia. MR angiography of the circle of Willis shows no abnormalities. Carotid Doppler ultrasonography discloses minimal stenosis in the common carotid arteries bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
correctExplanation: A variety of paraneoplastic neurologic syndromes may occur following an abnormal immune response to the presence of an underlying malignancy. The most implicated tumors are small cell lung carcinoma, breast and ovarian carcinoma, and Hodgkin lymphoma. In many cases, the onset of a paraneoplastic disorder may precede detection of the primary malignancy; therefore, patients may present without a known cancer history and a high index of suspicion for an occult tumor must be maintained. Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration (PCD) is a rare disorder characterized by dysfunction of the cerebellar vermis with signs and symptoms of ataxia, intention tremor, vertigo, nystagmus, dysarthria, and eventual loss of ambulation. A variety of autoantibodies may be detected in association with PCD, most commonly anti-Yo antibodies, which target an antigen specific to cerebellar Purkinje cells. MRI often shows cerebellar atrophy. Further diagnostic evaluation should be performed to identify the primary malignancy in a patient with suspected PCD.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (Choice A) is a human prion disease that presents with rapidly progressing dementia, neuropsychiatric symptoms, cerebellar dysfunction, corticospinal tract dysfunction, basal ganglia dysfunction, and stimulus-induced myoclonus. While Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease may cause a rapidly progressive dementia, this patient’s history of smoking, cough, and unintentional weight loss are suggestive of malignancy and a paraneoplastic disorder. Miller-Fisher syndrome (Choice B) is a subset of Guillain-Barré syndrome, an autoimmune demyelinating disorder. Miller-Fisher syndrome is characterized by the triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia. This contrasts with Guillain-Barré syndrome, which presents with acute-onset, ascending, bilateral muscle weakness. This patient has normal deep tendon reflexes, suggesting against the diagnosis. Multisystem atrophy (Choice C) is a parkinsonian, neurodegenerative disorder characterized by parkinsonism, autonomic dysfunction, and ataxia. Autonomic symptoms may include orthostatic hypotension, dry mouth, anhidrosis, urinary incontinence, and erectile dysfunction. Progressive supranuclear palsy (Choice E) is a parkinsonian, neurodegenerative disorder characterized by gait instability, oculomotor deficits (classically vertical gaze palsy), frontal lobe deficits, bradykinesia, and muscle rigidity. Wernicke encephalopathy (Choice F) results from vitamin B, (thiamine) deficiency and presents with the triad of encephalopathy, ataxia, and oculomotor dysfunction (typically nystagmus and horizontal gaze palsy). questionStem: Apreviously healthy 16-day-old male newborn is brought to the emergency department by his parents because of a 6-hour history of temperatures to 38.9°C (102°F), fussiness, and decreased feeding. He was born at 39 weeks’ gestation to a 32-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 2, and weighed 3090 g (6 Ib 13 oz) at birth. The mother received routine prenatal care. Pregnancy was complicated by group B streptococcal infection at 37 weeks’ gestation; no other abnormalities were noted on screening. The mother received three doses of intrapartum ampicillin. The patient was discharged on the second day of life. Well-child examinations on days 3 and 14 of life showed no abnormalities. At 2 weeks of age, he weighed 3232 g (7 lb 2 oz). He is currently breast-feeding. He has not had sick contacts. Today, he weighs 3260 g (7 Ib 3 oz). Head circumference is at the 50th percentile. His rectal temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F), pulse is 142/min and regular, respirations are 48/min, and blood pressure is 58/40 mm Hg. Examination shows no cyanosis or rash. The head is normocephalic with no signs of trauma. The anterior and posterior fontanels are open and ballotable; the anterior fontanel is not bulging. There is mild scleral icterus. The liver edge is palpated 1.5 cm below the right costal margin. The spleen is not palpable. The umbilical cord has detached; the site is dry and nonerythematous. A lumbar puncture is performed. Results of urinalysis and blood, urine, and cerebrospinal fluid cultures are pending. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Discharge after administration of a single dose of ceftriaxone

correctExplanation: Neonatal sepsis is often categorized on the basis of time from parturition, as the period of time in which symptoms begin may indicate which pathogen is likely involved, thereby guiding therapy. Early-onset neonatal sepsis occurs within 72 hours of birth, generally as a result of exposure to pathogens acquired from the mother, either through hematogenous or transplacental spread or, commonly, contact acquisition in the birth canal. Late-onset neonatal sepsis presents 72 hours or more after birth and is most likely acquired by contact with environmental pathogens, although those acquired from the mother are still possible. Neonatal sepsis often presents with symptoms of lethargy, fever, poor feeding, weak cry, and respiratory distress. The most common pathogens associated with late-onset neonatal sepsis include group B Streptococcus and Escherichia coli. Infants admitted to neonatal intensive care units are also at risk for other gram-negative bacteria, coagulase-negative Staphylococcus, and Staphylococcus aureus. Syndromes of serious bacterial infection include bacteremia, meningitis, and pneumonia. Workup for a suspected case of sepsis in a child younger than 30 days of age may include blood cultures, lumbar puncture, chest x-ray, complete blood count, and urinalysis, depending on the timing and nature of the patient’s symptoms. Treatment includes intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics to cover the common pathogens. The combination of ampicillin and gentamicin is preferred due to effective coverage against the most common causative agents of neonatal sepsis.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Discharge after administration of a single dose of ceftriaxone (Choice A) and admission to the hospital for observation only (Choice B) are incorrect, as this septic and hypotensive newborn requires intravenous antibiotics and further workup. Intramuscular ampicillin and gentamicin therapy (Choice C) could be an appropriate choice if the newborn required only one dose of antibiotics. This patient will require several days of antibiotics, and therefore intravenous administration is more appropriate as it avoids the need to re-stick the newborn multiple times. Intramuscular ceftriaxone therapy (Choice D) and intravenous ceftriaxone therapy (Choice F) are incorrect. Ceftriaxone should be avoided in newborns at risk for hyperbilirubinemia as it displaces bilirubin from albumin, increasing the free plasma concentrations of unconjugated bilirubin, and thereby increasing the risk for kernicterus. questionStem: An 18-year-old man comes to the office because of a 3-month history of increasingly severe left knee pain. The pain was originally mild and intermittent but has progressed to be severe and constant. He has noticed fullness in the area above the left knee during the past month; during the past 2 weeks, there has been increased difficulty walking and bearing weight on the affected leg. There is no recent history of trauma to the knee. He says that he "has not been feeling well overall" during the past month and that he has had a 2-kg (4.5-lb) unintentional weight loss because of decreased appetite. He has no other history of serious illness, and his only medication is ibuprofen as needed for partial pain relief. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 85/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 135/80 mm Hg. Physical examination shows erythema and tenderness of the left distal thigh and above the knee; there is limited flexion of the knee. An x-ray of the knee shows an area of medullary and cortical bone destruction with periosteal new bone formation at the diaphysial end of the lesion. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient's underlying condition?

choices.C: Knee brace placement and physical therapy
choices.D: F ) Oral vitamin D supplementation and bisphosphonate therapy

correctExplanation: Osteosarcoma is a rare, primary malignant tumor of the bone that affects the metaphysis of long bones. Osteosarcoma has a bimodal distribution, most frequently affecting adolescents and patients over age 60 years. Presenting symptoms include localized pain, pathologic fractures at the areas of involvement, and associated weight loss. Physical examination may show a large, tender, palpable soft tissue mass. Imaging, including x-ray and MRI, may be used to evaluate the extent of involvement. Standard of care for otherwise healthy patients with osteosarcoma includes surgical resection and chemotherapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Intramuscular corticosteroid injection (Choice A) may be used in the treatment of systemic inflammatory conditions. These injections are generally administered in the superior lateral buttocks to avoid injection into the sciatic nerve region. Intramuscular steroid injections are not used in the treatment of osteosarcoma. Intravenous antibiotic therapy (Choice B) is used in the treatment of septic arthritis and many infectious conditions. The most common causative microorganism in septic arthritis is Staphylococcus aureus. Antibiotics targeting S. aureus are often used as empiric antibiotic therapy. Knee brace placement and physical therapy (Choice C) are commonly used in the treatment of acute knee injuries and osteoarthritis. Knee braces provide added stability to the joint, while physical therapy aims to increase muscle strength and flexibility as well as prevent recurrent injury to the affected area. Oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug therapy (Choice E) such as naproxen is commonly used in the treatment of acute pain and osteoarthritis. These medications inhibit the COX enzyme. Adverse effects include gastritis, gastrointestinal bleeding, and nephropathy. They may be suitable adjuncts in cases of osteosarcoma but are not the primary treatment. Oral vitamin D supplementation and bisphosphonate therapy (Choice F) may be used in the treatment of osteoporosis. Osteoporosis is diagnosed by DEXA scan and is most common in postmenopausal female patients. Educational Objective: Osteosarcoma is a primary malignant tumor of the bone most frequently affecting adolescent and elderly patients. Patients may present with localized pain, pathologic fracture, and a palpable, tender mass on physical examination. Patients are evaluated with imaging studies and treated with surgical resection and chemotherapy. 4 a Previous Score Report Calculator

questionStem: A6/-year-old man with a 15-year history of emphysema comes to the office because of right-sided shoulder pain for 6 months. He has not had chest pain, palpitations, or headache. He has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 40 years. He has worked as a coal miner for 45 years. He appears older than his age. He is not in distress. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 92%. The left pupil is 3 mm, the right pupil is 2 mm; they both react to light. There is ptosis on the right. Examination shows decreased diaphragmatic excursion on the right and a prolonged expiratory phase. There is moderate clubbing of the fingers. Intrinsic muscles of the right hand are atrophic; muscle strength is 4/5 in the right upper extremity. X-ray of the chest shows a 3 x 4-cm right apical mass. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this patient's shoulder pain?

choices.A: Extrinsic compression of the spinal cord

correctExplanation: Bronchogenic carcinoma commonly presents with cough, weight loss, hemoptysis, and potential signs of bronchial obstruction such as wheezing or prolonged expiratory phase. If the carcinoma is located within the lung apex, referred to as a Pancoast tumor, it can infiltrate multiple adjacent structures such as the superior vena cava, subclavian vessels, sympathetic chain, recurrent laryngeal nerve, or brachial plexus. This can result in presenting features of Horner syndrome (unilateral ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis of the face), ipsilateral shoulder and upper extremity pain, and hoarseness. If the Pancoast tumor involves the right lung apex, superior vena cava syndrome may occur, which manifests with bilateral upper extremity and facial swelling, erythema, and vascular congestion caused by insufficient venous drainage from mass effect or vessel invasion. A Pancoast tumor typically presents as a consolidative, rounded mass in the lung apex on chest x-rays and CT scans.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Extrinsic compression of the spinal cord (Choice A) can occur with metastatic cancers to the spine or with an infection such as an epidural abscess, which can present with weakness and numbness in a dermatomal or myotomal distribution. It would be unlikely to cause Horner syndrome. Small cell carcinoma of the lung is a neoplasm of neuroendocrine cells and is associated with numerous paraneoplastic syndromes, including Cushing syndrome caused by increased production of ACTH (Choice B). ACTH produced by small cell carcinoma stimulates the adrenal gland zona fasciculata to increase the production of cortisol. Hypercortisolism, or Cushing syndrome, ensues with its many manifestations, including proximal muscle weakness, osteoporosis, hypertension, hyperglycemia, truncal obesity, moon facies, striae, amenorrhea, and/or immunosuppression. Squamous cell carcinoma is associated with hypercalcemia due to production of parathyroid-like hormone (also known as parathyroid hormone-related peptide) (Choice D). Hypercalcemia can present with nephrolithiasis, chronic bone pain, abdominal discomfort, and psychiatric disturbances. Jugular vein thrombosis (Choice E) would not compress adjacent structures and would be unlikely to cause Horner syndrome. Educational Objective: Pancoast tumors can infiltrate adjacent structures such as the superior vena cava, subclavian vessels, sympathetic chain, recurrent laryngeal nerve, or brachial plexus and can lead to Horner syndrome, ipsilateral shoulder and upper extremity pain, and hoarseness. questionStem: A 72-year-old man is brought to the physician because of a 1-year history of progressive difficulty walking and a 2-month history of urinary incontinence. His wife reports that he is extremely slow to answer questions. Neurologic examination shows bilateral grasp reflexes and increased muscle tone in all extremities. When he tries to walk, he appears "glued" to the floor and cannot take steps without assistance. He is oriented to person, place, and time but speaks very little. Which of the following is most likely to be increased in this patient?
correctExplanation: This patient presents with findings suggesting normal-pressure hydrocephalus (NPH), with the characteristic combination of dementia, gait instability, and urinary incontinence. NPH refers to a type of communicating (nonobstructive) hydrocephalus in which the ventricles are enlarged, leading to damage of the white matter tracts connecting the frontal lobes and basal ganglia. Patients commonly present with frontal cognitive deficits (eg, frontal release signs such as the reemergence of the grasp reflex) and subcortical cognitive deficits (eg, psychomotor slowing, inattention, executive dysfunction). Signs of increased intracranial pressure (eg, papilledema, postural headaches) are typically absent. Many cases of NPH are idiopathic though some are secondary to a defect in cerebrospinal fluid drainage from the ventricles due to scarring or obstruction of the ventricular lining from prior hemorrhage or meningitis. The diagnosis is primarily clinical, although ventriculomegaly on brain imaging is suggestive. The most appropriate next step in management is a lumbar puncture to assess the opening pressure and clinical response to removing cerebrospinal fluid. Placement of a ventricular shunt may be needed for long-term management.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Cerebrospinal fluid leukocyte count (Choice A) may be increased in meningitis and encephalitis, which commonly present acutely or subacutely with fever, headache, and altered mental status. This patient does not have a fever or headache, and his symptom onset was chronic and insidious. Cerebrospinal fluid pressure (Choice B) is likely to be normal in this patient as denoted by the name “normal-pressure hydrocephalus.” Excess cerebrospinal fluid collects in the ventricles but does not increase opening pressure. Opening pressure is often increased in meningitis and in idiopathic intracranial hypertension. Cortical sulci (Choice C) are increased in patients with neurodegenerative brain diseases such as dementia, Alzheimer type. In NPH, cortical sulci are not significantly increased. Striatal dopamine (Choice D) is increased by certain Parkinson disease medications. Dopamine dysregulation is not present in NPH. Educational Objective: Normal-pressure hydrocephalus refers to a type of communicating (nonobstructive) hydrocephalus in which the ventricles are enlarged, leading to damage of the white matter tracts connecting the frontal lobes and basal ganglia. questionStem: A 38-year-old woman comes to the clinic with her husband because she has had six episodes of severe abdominal pain during the past 4 months. She says when the episodes occur, the pain is continuous and located "all over my belly." During initial episodes, the pain persisted for 3 to 4 hours, but during more recent episodes, the pain has lasted 2 to 3 days. She rates the pain at its worst as an 8 on a 10-point scale. The episodes are accompanied by nausea, bloating, numbness in her hands and feet, severe burning pain in her thighs and calves, and severe constipation; these associated symptoms subside with the resolution of the abdominal pain. She also passed red urine after her most recent episode. Her husband says she often sweats during these episodes and he once measured her pulse rate at 100/min. The patient has no other history of serious illness and takes no medications. She has a family history of similar episodes in multiple relatives. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is most likely responsible for the color of this patient's urine?
correctExplanation: Acute intermittent porphyria is the most likely diagnosis for this patient with episodic abdominal pain and peripheral neuropathy in a “stocking-glove’” distribution, which is caused by an autosomal dominant mutation in the porphobilinogen deaminase gene HMBS. This enzyme catalyzes the third step in heme synthesis, which combines four porphobilinogen (PBG) molecules into hydroxymethylbilane, which is subsequently converted to uroporphyrinogen III. Loss of this enzyme leads to the accumulation of PBG, which is toxic to the nervous system. Additionally, increased activity of the upstream enzyme, delta-aminolevulinic acid synthase (ALAS1) leads to accumulation of aminolevulinic acid, which is also toxic. PBG accumulation in urine produces a reddish tinge and is also diagnostic when detected by urinalysis. The mutation affects both erythroid cells and hepatocytes. The disease’s manifestations are primarily neurologic and include peripheral neuropathy, bladder dysfunction, and autonomic dysfunction. Abdominal pain is classic and results often from ileus. The penetrance is low, so a family history is not often present, which can delay the diagnosis. Disease flares can occur after exposure to certain triggers, such as medications, tobacco, alcohol, stress, and starvation.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Carotene (Choice A) is a naturally occurring pigment that is converted into vitamin A. It is found in many plants, such as carrots, pumpkins, and sweet potatoes, and in many vitamin supplements. It may cause a harmless, orange urinary discoloration when consumed in excess, but does not produce neurologic or gastrointestinal symptoms. Hemoglobin (Choice B) may impart a reddish discoloration to urine in association with a variety of autoimmune, infectious, inflammatory, and coagulation disorders (eg, paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura). However, this patient's presentation is most suggestive of acute intermittent porphyria, which does not cause hemoglobinuria. questionStem: A previously healthy 24-year-old man is brought to the physician because of a 3-day history of progressive loss of vision in the right eye and pain behind the eye with movement. He has no history of similar symptoms. Funduscopic examination shows no abnormalities. Visual acuity is 20/100 on the right. Visual field testing shows a right central scotoma. There is a right afferent pupillary defect. Over the next 10 years, this patient is at greatest risk for which of the following conditions?
correctExplanation: Optic neuritis results from autoimmune demyelinating inflammation of the optic nerve and presents in young, often female patients with unilateral vision loss and pain that is exacerbated with extraocular movements. Ocular examination discloses decreased visual acuity and color vision, a relative afferent pupillary defect, and possible optic disc edema. Diagnosis is confirmed with fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) MRI sequences showing hyperintensity of the optic nerve. Patients with optic neuritis are at increased risk for multiple sclerosis (MS), and optic neuritis is a common initial finding in patients with MS. Recently, autoantibodies against myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) and aquaporin-4 (AQP4) have been identified as causative of some cases of optic neuritis. Patients who develop optic neuritis due to antibodies against MOG and AQP4 often have severe presentations but also have decreased risk for subsequent MS compared with patients with optic neuritis who lack these autoantibodies. The Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial demonstrated that a short course of treatment with high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone speeds up the rate of visual recovery and delays the onset of MS, although it does not impact final visual acuity. It also demonstrated that the presence and quantity of periventricular white matter lesions on MRI is the most important prognostic risk factor for the subsequent development of MS.

Diabetes mellitus, anticholinergic medications, and Sturge-Weber syndrome have all been associated with increased risk for glaucoma. Graves ophthalmopathy (Choice B) may present with exophthalmos, eyelid retraction, and lid lag, and is associated with Graves disease. Herpes encephalitis (Choice C) may present with headache, confusion, fever, and seizures. It is most commonly caused by herpes simplex virus 1. Macular degeneration (Choice D) may present with insidious blurring of central vision and metamorphopsia. Advanced age is the biggest risk factor associated with developing macular degeneration. Myotonic dystrophy (Choice F) typically presents with muscle weakness, myotonia, cataracts, frontal balding, cardiac arrhythmias, and hypogonadism. The most frequently affected muscles include the facial muscles, sternocleidomastoid, distal forearm muscles, intrinsic hand muscles, and ankle dorsiflexors. It is a genetic condition caused by a trinucleotide repeat. Temporal arteritis (Choice G) is a vasculitis of medium and large vessels in elderly patients that commonly presents with headache, jaw claudication, and proximal muscle stiffness. questionStem: A56-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance 1 hour after he was found by his neighbor sitting in the hallway of his apartment building and speaking unintelligibly. On admission, the patient is confused and somnolent; he is unable to provide a medical history. He has alcohol-related cirrhosis complicated by bleeding from esophageal varices, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis. His medications are spironolactone, furosemide, nadolol, and ursodiol. During his last clinic visit 2 weeks ago, the patient stated that he has remained abstinent from alcohol use. His examination at that time showed mild confusion. Today, the patient appears somnolent but is easily aroused. He is 175 cm (5 ft 9 in) tall and weighs 56 kg (123 Ib); BMI is 18 kg/m2. Temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 78/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 114/72 mm Hg. Physical examination shows palmar erythema and gynecomastia. The abdomen is protuberant with caput medusae radiating from the umbilicus. When asked to outstretch his arms with wrists extended, the patient's hands transiently drop forward in a nonrhythmic manner. Mental status examination shows a reduced attention span. He is oriented to person but not to place, time, or situation. Results of laboratory studies are shown: Hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL Hematocrit 34% Leukocyte count 7800/mm3 Serum Nat 133 mEq/L K* 3.2 MEq/L Urea nitrogen 14 mg/dL Creatinine 1.2 mg/dL Ammonia 54 yg/dL Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy at this time?
correctExplanation: Hepatic encephalopathy is commonly associated with decompensated liver cirrhosis. Signs of hepatic encephalopathy include confusion, stupor, asterixis, tremor, and myoclonus on physical examination. Hepatic encephalopathy results from accumulation of ammonia produced by colonic bacteria. Serum ammonia concentrations in patients with hepatic encephalopathy may be increased, though this is not necessary for the diagnosis. Treatments for hepatic encephalopathy include rifaximin and lactulose. Rifaximin is a gut-selective, nonabsorbable antibiotic with activity against gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria. questionStem: A46-year-old woman comes to the emergency department 18 hours after the sudden onset of severe, intermittent, left-sided facial pain. She describes the pain as "an electric jolt that turns on and off every minute." The pain started while she was brushing her teeth the previous evening and is localized to the left premolar area of the upper dental arch. She reports that ibuprofen relieved the pain for 3 hours, but the pain recurred this morning when she rinsed her mouth with cold water. She has hypertension and multiple sclerosis. Her medications are metoprolol, lisinopril, and fingolimod. Her maternal aunt also has multiple sclerosis. The patient appears anxious and occasionally winces in pain. Temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 64/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 146/88 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following reflexes should be tested in order to determine if further diagnostic studies are indicated at this time?
correctExplanation: Trigeminal neuralgia is a neuropathic pain disorder that presents with severe shooting or burning pain within the innervated regions of the sensory branches of the trigeminal nerve. The trigeminal nerve divides into three sensory branches, V1 to V3, which innervate the forehead (V1) and the skin overlying the zygomatic and maxillary bone (V2) and the mandible (V3). The pathophysiology of the pain is believed to be related to compression of the trigeminal nerve by adjacent blood vessels or bone as it exits the skull base. Symptoms may be triggered by light touch, shaving, or swallowing, or may occur without any precipitant. The pain is generally described as severe. The trigeminal nerve also mediates the corneal reflex, which involves blinking of the eyelids caused by stimulation of the cornea. Trigeminal neuralgia is associated with loss of the corneal reflex. Treatment includes carbamazepine or surgical decompression.

The palmomental reflex (Choice C) is a primitive reflex present in neonates and infants that involves an involuntary contraction of the mentalis muscle of the mandible elicited by stimulation of the thenar eminence. The pupillary light reflex (Choice D) involves the optic nerve and the oculomotor nerve and causes constriction of the pupils in response to light. Loss of the pupillary light reflex can occur in the setting of an optic nerve injury, brainstem lesion, or oculomotor nerve injury. The visual threat reflex (Choice E) involves involuntary blinking in response to a visual threat and is associated with the optic nerve. questionStem: A33-year-old woman comes to the physician 24 hours after a fainting episode. Menses have occurred at irregular intervals over the past 6 months. She has had numbing and tingling of her left hand for 2 years. She has had intermittent episodes of sharp, stabbing lower abdominal pain over the past 5 years; she has had no nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or constipation. Treatment with acetaminophen, ibuprofen, and codeine has been ineffective. Three exploratory laparoscopies did not disclose the cause of the pain, and surgical treatment for uterine adhesions did not provide any significant relief. She has a history of multiple sexual partners but has abstained for the past 3 years because of dyspareunia. Her blood pressure is 140/84 mm Hg. The abdomen is moderately tender to light and deep palpation with no rebound tenderness. Bowel sounds are active. Pelvic examination is difficult to perform because of increased cervical pain. There is bilateral tenderness on palpation of the ovaries. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: This patient with numerous non-specific symptoms with no medical explanation after extensive workup has a presentation concerning for somatization disorder. In somatization disorder, or somatic symptom disorder, the patient is excessively preoccupied with one or more somatic symptoms such that these symptoms disrupt the patient's daily life. These symptoms may or may not originate from an underlying disease, though they are typically unconsciously produced or exacerbated by psychological factors such as stress. Patients persistently devote excessive time and energy to these symptoms or related health concerns (eg, repeatedly going to the doctor). Patients often undergo extensive diagnostic testing that is unrevealing. Management of somatic symptom disorder centers around regular primary care follow-up that targets coping skills, provides reassurance, and avoids unnecessary tests.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Conversion disorder (Choice A), also known as functional neurologic symptom disorder, involves neurologic symptoms such as sensory or motor dysfunction that are not fully explained by objective findings on physical examination or imaging. Functional neurologic symptom disorder is postulated to represent the subconscious conversion of intolerable emotional distress into physical symptoms. Crohn disease (Choice B) is characterized by transmural inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract and presents with abdominal pain, bloody or watery diarrhea, low-grade fever, and weight loss. Pelvic pain, dyspareunia, and numbness are not consistent with a diagnosis of Crohn disease. Endometriosis (Choice C) is caused by ectopic endometrial tissue outside the uterus and presents with chronic dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, dyschezia, and infertility. Symptoms are typically cyclical. The gold standard for diagnosis is diagnostic laparoscopy, which evaluates for endometriotic implant lesions on the peritoneum. This patient has had three laparoscopies that did not show ectopic endometrial tissue. Illness anxiety disorder (Choice D) is characterized by persistent excessive anxiety about having or acquiring a serious illness despite negative diagnostic testing. These patients often experience minimal symptoms and have normal physical examinations. This patient has a preoccupation with her symptoms rather than a specific diagnosis. Educational Objective: Somatization disorder is characterized by excessive preoccupation with one or more somatic symptoms such that these symptoms disrupt the patient's daily life. Patients persistently devote excessive time and energy to these symptoms or related health concerns (eg, repeatedly going to the doctor). 4 e Previous Score Report Calculator

questionStem: A5/-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of progressive hearing loss in his left ear. He initially only had difficulty hearing while talking on the telephone, but now he has difficulty hearing most of the time. During this period, he occasionally has had a 30-second episode of unsteadiness and a spinning sensation. He has been otherwise healthy. Examination shows flattening of the left nasolabial fold and decreased wrinkling of the forehead on the left side. There is rotatory nystagmus on right lateral gaze and profound sensorineural hearing loss on the left. Mental status examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely location of the lesion?
correctExplanation: Acoustic neuromas are tumors derived from Schwann cells involving the vestibulocochlear nerve. The vestibulocochlear nerve originates between the pons and medulla oblongata and exits the brainstem near the cerebellopontine angle. Symptoms associated with the development of an acoustic neuroma include hearing loss and tinnitus associated with the cochlear nerve as well as gait instability and vertigo associated with the vestibular nerve. As tumors enlarge there may be involvement of the trigeminal nerve or facial nerve. Patients with neurofibromatosis 2 may present with bilateral acoustic neuromas. Imaging studies, including CT scan or MRI, can be used to make the diagnosis. Treatment options include surgical resection or radiation therapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Brain stem tegmentum (Choice A) is the portion of the brainstem ventral to the cerebral aqueduct and fourth ventricle. This area would not be affected by an acoustic neuroma. Cochlea (Choice C) is a component of the inner ear and plays a role in the sensation of hearing and transducing auditory signals to the brain. Patients with damage to the cochlea experience sensorineural hearing loss. Mastoid bone (Choice D) is located posterior to the ear and contains mastoid air cells. This area is a potential space for infection in patients with fever of unknown origin or following prolonged or spreading otitis media. Mastoiditis, or inflammation of the mastoid bone, would not cause this patient's symptoms. Temporal lobe (Choice E) contributes to the cerebral cortex and is associated with auditory perception, language recognition, comprehension, and speech. A lesion involving the Wernicke area of the temporal lobe results in Wernicke aphasia where patients can produce speech though it is often garbled and inappropriate. The vestibulocochlear nerve originates between the pons and medulla oblongata and exits the brainstem near the cerebellopontine angle. questionStem: An 82-year-old woman is brought to the physician because of a 3-month history of brief memory loss two to three times weekly. She also has had difficulty maintaining her balance. She has glaucoma, hyperlipidemia, and hypertension. Her medications are pilocarpine eyedrops, losartan, and atorvastatin. Her pulse is 92/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 132/84 mm Hg. Examination shows arcus senilis and slight restriction of upward gaze. Deep tendon reflexes are decreased at the ankles compared with the knees. On gait testing, she walks flexed at the waist and is unable to tandem walk. On mental status examination, she is fully oriented. She performs serial sevens without difficulty. Her immediate, recent, and remote memory is intact. She displays normal abstract thinking. Which of the following best explains this patient's neurologic findings?
correctExplanation: This patient with brief episodic memory loss, arcus senilis, decreased Achilles reflexes, and flexed posture is showing signs of psychomotor slowing consistent with normal aging. Normal aging includes a slow decline of executive functioning, attention span, and problem-solving after age 70 years. Other findings consistent with aging include decreased or absent Achilles reflex, arcus senilis (grey or white arch visible around the outer edge of the cornea), decreased vision and hearing, decreased immune response, and increased suicide rate. Despite these common changes, an individual experiencing normal aging should still be able to function in society.

questionStem: Apreviously healthy 37-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital because of a 3-day history of weakness of her arms and legs. Her symptoms began 6 days ago with backache and a prickling sensation in her legs. She is alert and oriented. Vital signs are within normal limits. Cranial nerves are intact. Muscle strength is 3/5 in the distal upper and lower extremities and 4/5 in the proximal upper and lower extremities. She is unable to walk without assistance. Sensation to pinprick is decreased below the knees. Deep tendon reflexes are absent in the Achilles and patellar tendons bilaterally. Babinski sign is absent bilaterally. In GBS, a preceding infection (eg, Campylobacter jejuni, influenza-like illnesses) leads to autoimmune cross-reactivity with the myelin of the nerve roots exiting the spinal cord. The ventral nerve roots, containing motor and sympathetic efferents, are most commonly involved, though the dorsal nerve roots (controlling sensation) may also be affected. As such, patients typically present with acute symmetric muscle weakness with depressed or absent deep tendon reflexes (reflecting a lower motor neuron pattern of dysfunction) that begins in the lower extremities and may rapidly ascend to involve the upper extremities, bulbar muscles, and/or respiratory muscles. Autonomic dysfunction (eg, blood pressure fluctuations, cardiac irregularities) is common. Sensory deficits and pain can also occur, though these symptoms are typically mild compared with motor dysfunction. The diagnosis is confirmed by increased cerebrospinal fluid protein with normal cell counts on lumbar puncture, termed albuminocytologic dissociation, thought to reflect generalized inflammation. Management includes respiratory support and, for severe cases, plasma exchange or intravenous immunoglobulin therapy. Intravenous immunoglobulin therapy may work by neutralizing the cross-reactive antibodies that cause GBS.

questionStem: A5/-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after his wife was unable to arouse him from sleep. He has hypertension but is currently taking no medications. His blood pressure is 190/100 mm Hg. Examination shows both eyes deviated to the left. He does not withdraw his right upper and lower extremities to painful stimuli. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

ICH can occur in patients with chronic hypertension, typically due to hemorrhage from small penetrating arteries in the pons, midbrain, thalamus, putamen, caudate, or cerebellum. Risk factors for hypertensive ICH include uncontrolled hypertension and antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy, such as with aspirin or warfarin. Patients can present with headache, vomiting, confusion, altered mental status, stupor, or coma. Focal neurologic deficits depend on the site of the ICH and can include hemiparesis, hemisensory symptoms, gaze palsy, dysarthria, aphasia, or if in the cerebellum, ataxia, vomiting, and disequilibrium. Patients may manifest upper motor neuron examination findings such as spasticity, hyperreflexia, and extensor plantar reflex (Babinski sign). Diagnosis is made with noncontrast CT scan of the head, which will show hyperdense intraparenchymal acute blood products.

questionStem: A63-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of a 3-hour history of double vision. She also has a 1-week history of moderate pain and numbness around her right eye. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Examination shows exophthalmos of the right eye. When asked to look to the right, the patient reports double vision; the right eye does not fully abduct. Sensation to pinprick is decreased over the right forehead and below the right eye. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Cavernous sinus thrombosis classically follows an infection or injury involving a structure drained by the cavernous sinus and results in cranial nerve deficits involving those that traverse the cavernous sinus (Ill, IV, V1, V2, or VI). Causes include sinusitis, orbital cellulitis, dental infections, pharyngitis, and cellulitis or abscess, especially within the danger triangle of the face (formed by the apex of the nose and the corners of the mouth). Features include fever, orbit pain, exophthalmos, periorbital edema, impaired pupil reactivity, and impaired extraocular movement, causing diplopia. Impaired corneal reflex and sensation in the V1 and/or V2 distribution can also occur. When the cause is orbital cellulitis, patients may additionally present with pain with extraocular movements and optic nerve dysfunction, which can be suggested by the presence of decreased color perception, a relative afferent pupillary defect, or optic disc edema. Patients in whom cavernous sinus thrombosis is suspected should undergo urgent CT venography or contrast-enhanced MR venography. Treatment involves anticoagulation, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and antifungals. Even with prompt recognition and appropriate treatment, the burden of long-term complications, including visual impairment and stroke, remains high.

While this patient has exophthalmos, she lacks other systemic signs of Graves disease. questionStem: Apreviously healthy 3-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 3-day history of decreased feeding. He also has a 1-day history of cough that worsens when he attempts to feed. His mother reports that he seems hungry but "tires out" while feeding. He was born at 40 weeks' gestation to a 25-year-old primigravid woman following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. He weighed 3600 g (7 Ib 15 oz) at birth. Until 1 week ago, he had been exclusively breast-fed; he now receives cow milk-based formula. The patient's father has been excavating the soil around the house to build a foundation for an additional room. On examination, the patient is alert and quiet and has a weak cry. He is at the 50th percentile for length and weight. His temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 138/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 72/48 mm Hg. Examination of the skin shows no abnormalities. Facial expression is absent. The pupils are 5 mm and sluggishly reactive. The gag reflex is decreased. Transmitted upper airway noises are heard. No murmurs are heard. Abdominal examination shows no abnormalities. Peripheral pulses are 2+ and symmetric. There is head lag and no spontaneous movement of the extremities. Muscle tone is decreased. Deep tendon reflexes are normal. Which of the following is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
correctExplanation: This patient with difficulty feeding, hypotonia, and facial muscle weakness has a presentation concerning for infantile botulism. Botulism is an acute disease of the neuromuscular junctio caused by exposure to the Clostridium botulinum toxin. C. botulinum is a gram-positive, spore-forming, obligate anaerobic bacterium. It produces botulinum toxin, a potent neurotoxin tha is absorbed into the end-terminal of cholinergic motor neurons, where it cleaves SNARE proteins, thereby preventing the release of acetylcholine vesicles into the neuromuscular junction. Botulism is often encountered as a food-borne illness through contaminated food products. Historically, C. botulinum was responsible for outbreaks of “sausage poisoning” through contaminated ham products and acquired its name after the Latin for sausage, “botulus.” In the modern era, it is more often responsible for poisoning via the ingestion of raw honey or canned foods. In infants, infection most commonly occurs through inhalation of spores from contaminated soil or dust; however, a common route of exposure is the ingestion of spores in honey when a parent feeds it to a child. The infant gastrointestinal flora is not sufficiently mature to prevent infection. Botulism presents with rapidly progressive, symmetric hypotonia and hyporeflexia that begins with the cranial nerves, manifesting as ptosis, sluggish pupils, and a diminished gag reflex, and descends to the lower extremities, also causing constipation, poor feeding, and respiratory failure. Diagnosis is confirmed by identification of the botulinum toxin in the stool. Treatment requires hospitalization and administration of immune globulin, as well as supportive care, which often includes mechanical ventilation.

Patients classically present with diarrhea, urination, miosis, bronchospasm, bradycardia, vomiting, lacrimation, and salivation. Measurement of negative inspiratory force (NIF) (Choice C) can be performed to assess respiratory muscle strength in patients with muscular weakness. A low NIF may indicate that a patient is at risk for respiratory muscle fatigue and decompensation and may necessitate respiratory support. Patients with botulism may develop diaphragmatic weakness and therefore may have a low NIF, but this is a nonspecific finding and is not diagnostic for any one disease. Additionally, measurement of NIF requires patient participation (patient is instructed to fully inhale), which would not be possible for this 3-month-old patient. questionStem: A9-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after being involved in a motor vehicle collision. There is an open fracture of the tibial shaft, and the patient reports severe pain in the area surrounding the fracture. On examination, there is weakness of toe flexion, severe pain with passive extension of the toes, and plantar hyperesthesia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Compartment syndrome occurs when there is increased pressure in the intramuscular compartment that compromises circulation and neuromuscular and neurologic function. Compartment syndrome commonly occurs in the setting of trauma, including long bone fractures, and symptoms include pain out of proportion to the injury, paresthesia, and pain with passive stretching of the muscles. Late findings are pallor, pulselessness, and paralysis. Diagnosis is confirmed after clinical suspicion by measuring compartment pressures. Increased compartment pressure or minimal difference between compartment pressure and perfusing blood pressures confirm the diagnosis. Treatment with ibuprofen relieves the headaches. She has had a 23-kg (50-lb) weight gain and menstrual irregularity over the past year. Menses now occur at irregular 20- to 90-day intervals. questionStem: After renovating a new home, a 41-year-old woman has burning pain and tingling in her right index, long, and ring fingers, particularly at night. The thenar eminence becomes atrophied. Which of the following structures is most likely to be damaged?
correctExplanation: Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) results from compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel and presents with signs and symptoms including pain, weakness, and paresthesia of the first three digits and the lateral half of the fourth digit, along with positive provocative test maneuvers such as the Tinel or Phalen tests. The carpal tunnel is located anterior to the carpal bones and is bound by the flexor retinaculum. The flexor tendons of the fingers course through the tunnel, along with the median nerve. The space is rigid and does not generally permit compression; thus, any inflammatory, traumatic, or space-filling lesion may result in CTS. Patients generally present with pain and paresthesia in the median nerve distribution, along with weakness involving the muscles of the thenar eminence that eventually may atrophy. Symptoms are generally worse at night and relieved with shaking of the hands. CTS is frequently associated with pregnancy, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, acromegaly, amyloidosis, ganglion cysts, obesity, and acute trauma to the wrist with impingement, or chronic remodeling and scar formation following a wrist injury. Patients with mild symptoms can be treated conservatively with wrist splinting. Wrist splints are typically worn at night but may also be used during the day. Splinting reduces the range of motion of the wrist and limits activities that increase pressure within the carpal tunnel. Patients who have persistent or severe symptoms or muscular weakness may require surgical decompression.

The radial nerve (Choice D) courses posterior to the humerus at the midshaft within the radial groove. It is often injured in displaced midshaft humerus fractures, with resulting wrist drop. The radial nerve supplies motor fibers to the triceps brachii and the extensor muscles within the posterior compartment of the forearm, and sensory fibers to the dorsum of the forearm, wrist, and hand. The ulnar nerve (Choice E) supplies motor fibers to the intrinsic muscles of the hand, and sensation over the anteromedial ring and small fingers and medial palm including hypothenar eminence. Damage to the roots or to the nerve along its course (eg, in the cubital tunnel) can result in motor dysfunction of the fingers, and numbness or paresthesia involving the medial aspect of the upper extremity. He has had approximately five episodes of visual loss in the right eye over the past 3 weeks that lasted less than 1 hour. He has hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Patients may have a history of preceding amaurosis fugax. Examination shows profound diminishment of visual acuity, a relative afferent pupillary defect, and a pale fundus with preserved foveal color. CRAO is a medical emergency, as it is an ischemic stroke of the ophthalmic vasculature and indicates a high risk for associated ischemic stroke to the brain. Patients who present with CRAO should be admitted to a stroke center for emergent evaluation, including a search for a possible embolic source with echocardiography and duplex ultrasonography of the carotid arteries. A careful history and laboratory evaluation of ESR, serum C-reactive protein concentration, and platelet count should be performed to evaluate for possible temporal arteritis. There is no proven medical or surgical therapy for CRAO, and the visual prognosis is poor.

In advanced stages, vision loss may result from retinal geographic atrophy or choroidal neovascularization with macular edema, exudation, or hemorrhage. Risk factors include age, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, smoking, diabetes mellitus, coagulopathy or blood dyscrasia, and increased intraocular pressure. She has a 25-year history of occasional throbbing headaches. The headaches occur once or twice annually, are associated with nausea and vomiting, and are relieved with sleep. She has hypertension treated with enalapril. On arrival, she can answer questions but is intermittently listless and agitated. Her temperature is 37.7°C (99.8°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 154/96 mm Hg. On examination, the left pupil is larger than the right. The left eye deviates slightly downward and outward. The patient resists flexion of the neck and exhibits pain when the neck is flexed. Muscle tone in the right upper and lower extremities is increased. Deep tendon reflexes on the right side are increased. Babinski sign is present on the right. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: A ruptured intracerebral aneurysm is the most common cause of nontraumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). Saccular intracerebral aneurysms typically occur at bifurcations in the circle of Willis, most commonly at the site of the anterior communicating artery. Aneurysms can also be associated with hereditary diseases such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. This patient presents in a nontraumatic, altered mental state with findings concerning for increased intracranial pressure with herniation. This patient's focal neurologic findings and asymmetric pupils are concerning for possible transtentorial herniation. SAH results from bleeding into the subarachnoid space. Patients may present with an acute, severe headache, stupor, or coma in severe cases. Blood in the subarachnoid space irritates the meninges, leading to nuchal rigidity. CT scan of the head shows hyperdense blood products in the cerebral sulci and basal cisterns. As the blood products circulate within the subarachnoid space, complications include the development of communicating hydrocephalus in the acute stage, along with rebleeding and vasospasm in the week following the initial bleed.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Carotid artery dissection with embolization (Choice A) can lead to focal neurologic deficits such as with an acute ischemic stroke and upper motor neuron signs such as increased deep tendon reflexes and Babinski sign. However, it would be unlikely to cause nuchal rigidity. Uncontrolled hypertension can lead to intracranial hemorrhage (Choice B), which presents with a progressively worsening headache and focal neurologic deficits. Hypertension leads to intraparenchymal hemorrhages typically in the basal ganglia, cerebellum, thalamus, and/or pons. Nuchal rigidity would be unlikely, and this patient’s blood pressure discloses mild (not severe) hypertension. While patients with meningoencephalitis (Choice C) often present with acute headache and neck stiffness, the absence of fever makes it less likely. Pupil asymmetry is concerning for increased intracranial pressure and herniation, which would be unlikely with meningoencephalitis. Migraine headaches characteristically recur over time and may present with a pulsatile, unilateral or bilateral headache with associated photophobia or phonophobia. They are often triggered by foods, medications, noises, menses, or illness. Vertebrobasilar migraines (Choice E) can also be associated with diplopia, dysarthria, nausea, or vomiting. Educational Objective: The most common cause of nontraumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage is a ruptured intracerebral aneurysm. questionStem: A4/-year-old man has to quit his job as an automobile mechanic because of hand weakness and unsteadiness. He has bilateral wristdrop and upper limb ataxia. Laboratory studies show: Hematocrit 34% Mean corpuscular volume 76 ums Serum creatinine 2 mg/dL Chronic exposure to which of the following substances is the most likely explanation for these findings?
correctExplanation: Symptoms of acute lead poisoning occur within days or weeks of exposure and include abdominal pain, constipation, arthralgia, myalgias, muscle weakness, excessive fatigue, headache, and difficulty concentrating. With prolonged exposure, chronic neurologic symptoms such as decline in cognition, depression, distal motor neuropathy, decreased hearing, tremor, and decreased brain volume on imaging may be present. The distal motor neuropathy causes lower motor neuron signs such as atrophy of muscles and hyporeflexia, as found in this patient. Microcytic anemia is also common, since lead inhibits the enzymes ferrochelatase and 5-aminolevulinic acid (6-ALA) dehydratase, resulting in decreased heme synthesis. In adults, exposure to lead primarily comes through occupation and/or hobbies. Individuals working with batteries, mining, construction, or ammunition are at higher risk. Diagnosis is suspected based on exposure and symptoms and is confirmed with increased serum lead concentration. Management of lead poisoning depends on the blood lead concentration and presence of symptoms, and includes chelation with dimercaprol, ethylene diamine tetraacetate, or succimer. Sources of lead should be investigated and eliminated.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Arsenic (Choice A) poisoning is uncommon and can cause dermatitis, skin cancer, neuropathy, hepatotoxicity, and, in severe cases, systemic toxicity and death. Acute large exposure to arsenic can cause gastrointestinal distress, QT prolongation that may progress to torsades de pointes, cardiac arrhythmias, shock, and acute respiratory distress syndrome. Cadmium (Choice B) poisoning may occur in the industrial setting among workers involved in electroplating, metallurgical industries, and battery production. Exposure typically occurs via inhalation and presents with fever, chills, myalgia, chest pain, cough, shortness of breath, pneumonitis, and pulmonary edema. Mercury (Choice D) poisoning may occur in an industrial setting among workers involved in the manufacture of thermometers, mirrors, fluorescent lighting, and gold. Patients present with headache, ataxia, tremor, hearing and vision loss, insomnia, peripheral neuropathy, and paresthesias. Thallium (Choice E) poisoning may occur through transcutaneous exposure or via inhalation or ingestion. Thallium was previously widely used as a rodenticide, but thallium poisoning is now rare in the developed world, although it is still used in the manufacture of semiconductors, electronics, and optics. Acute exposure presents with abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting, while chronic exposure presents with neurologic and psychiatric symptoms of headache, altered mental status, anxiety, psychosis, ataxia, tremor, and painful peripheral neuropathy and distal weakness. Educational Objective: Neurologic manifestations of lead poisoning include cognitive dysfunction, encephalopathy, hearing loss, and peripheral neuropathy. questionStem: A27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-day history of difficulty speaking and moving. Seven days ago she began a course of mitoxantrone and high doses of cytarabine (ara-C) for a recurrence of acute myeloid leukemia. She has been lethargic and mildly confused for the past 24 hours. She is 140 cm (4 ft 7 in) tall and weighs 47 kg (103 Ib); BMI is 24 kg/m2. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 72/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Examination shows nystagmus and ataxic eye movements. Muscle strength is full, but there is marked ataxia in all extremities. She is unable to maintain her balance sitting or standing unsupported. She is somnolent but can respond appropriately to questions and instructions. Her speech is irregular in rate and volume. Language function and memory are normal. She can calculate well, and her abstract reasoning is intact. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.E: Spread of leukemia to the central nervous system

correctExplanation: Acute-onset neurologic findings in the setting of recent chemotherapy are concerning for drug toxicity. Specifically, nystagmus, ataxia, impaired coordination, postural instability, and dysarthria or other speech abnormalities, in the setting of intact strength and higher cognitive functions are indicative of cerebellar dysfunction. Cytarabine, a pyrimidine analog, can cause loss of Purkinje cells in the cerebellum, leading to acute cerebellar syndrome. Risk factors include underlying neurologic dysfunction and impaired hepatic or renal function. Patients who present with acute cerebellar syndrome should discontinue cytarabine immediately. Some may experience permanent deficits, while others may experience spontaneous resolution.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Cerebral infarction (Choice A) can present with a sudden change in mental status, upper motor neuron signs, and acute focal neurologic deficits, especially on one side of the body, and may have speech difficulty, dysarthria, or aphasia, depending on the territory involved. Cerebellar strokes, while less common, do occur. However, acute-onset cerebellar signs in the setting of a new course of cytarabine are more likely caused by drug toxicity. Encephalitis (Choice C) presents with fever, altered mental status, and neurologic abnormalities, such as seizure, aphasia, hemiparesis, or cranial nerve deficits. Neuroimaging will typically show changes in the temporal lobe. Encephalitis is commonly associated with nuchal rigidity or signs of central nervous system infection, which this patient does not demonstrate, making it a less likely cause of her presentation. Intracranial hemorrhage (Choice D) appears as a hyperdense collection of blood within the brain parenchyma on CT scan. Intracranial hemorrhage often presents with focal neurologic deficits based on its location with an associated headache and symptoms of increased intracranial pressure (eg, vomiting, altered mental status). This patient does not demonstrate any signs of increased intracranial pressure. Spread of leukemia to the central nervous system (Choice E), also called leukemic meningitis, is usually asymptomatic. When it does occur, signs and symptoms vary widely depending on the location of spread, and can include headache, signs of increased intracranial pressure, behavioral changes, and focal weakness. Isolated cerebellar signs in the setting of recently started cytarabine is more consistent with drug toxicity. Educational Objective: Cytarabine, a pyrimidine analog, can cause loss of Purkinje cells in the cerebellum, leading to acute cerebellar syndrome. Features include nystagmus, ataxia, impaired coordination, postural instability, and dysarthria or other speech abnormalities. Strength, sensation, and higher cognitive functions are intact. Patients who present with acute cerebellar syndrome should discontinue cytarabine immediately. questionStem: A6/-year-old woman with a 15-year history of Parkinson disease comes to the office because of increasing involuntary movements over the past 2 years. She also has had nausea from her medication regimen of carbidopa-levodopa and ropinirole; attempts at medication adjustment have not been successful. She also has a long-standing history of cervical and lumbar stenosis treated with diclofenac and physical therapy. Her pulse is 70/min and blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg while sitting; pulse is 75/min and blood pressure is 80/50 mm Hg while standing. Her speech is barely audible. Examination shows constant writhing movements of the mouth, neck, and limbs. She walks with her neck flexed and takes small steps with a decreased arm swing. Mental status examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate surgical treatment?
correctExplanation: Parkinson disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by degradation of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra. Symptoms are associated with an imbalance of dopamine and acetylcholine, resulting in the characteristic findings of bradykinesia, resting tremor, muscle rigidity, and postural instability. Psychiatric disturbances, sleep disorders, and dementia are common complications in addition to prominent motor symptoms. Initial pharmacologic management of Parkinson disease consists of carbidopa-levodopa and/or other dopamine agonists such as pramipexole and ropinirole. Patients who develop severe, disabling motor symptoms refractory to medications and physical therapy may be considered for device-assisted therapies or invasive lesioning procedures. Device-assisted therapies include deep brain stimulation. Invasive lesioning procedures are more common for patients who do not have access to device-assisted therapies or cannot afford them. Unilateral pallidotomy, which targets the internal globus pallidus to reduce inhibitory signaling, is an effective treatment for improving refractory tremor, bradykinesia, dyskinesia, chorea, and gait/balance instability. The thalamus and subthalamic nucleus are alternative targets for lesioning procedures.

His wife says that he has been experiencing visual hallucinations. He refuses to drink liquids. For 3 days prior to this behavior, he had headache and sleepiness. Two months ago, he returned from a hunting trip in the mountains. His temperature is 40°C (104°F). Examination shows an inability to accurately answer questions and unusual behaviors such as picking at the air. He seems unable to swallow his secretions, and he is drooling. ACT scan of the brain shows no abnormalities. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis shows: Glucose 70 mg/dL Protein 85 mg/dL Leukocyte count 150/mm3 Erythrocyte count none Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

In the United States, transmission occurs most often after a bite from a bat, raccoon, or skunk, but in third-world countries, transmission via dog bites is common. The virus has a long incubation period of weeks to months before symptom onset. It binds to acetylcholine receptors in peripheral nerves and travels up the axon in a retrograde fashion to the central nervous system. Initial symptoms include headache, fever, and malaise, but rapidly progress to agitation, photophobia, hydrophobia, and hypersalivation. Once symptoms are present, rabies is almost universally fatal. For this reason, persons who are bit by an animal at high risk for carrying rabies should seek care immediately. Copious irrigation of the wound followed by intramuscular administration of the killed vaccine is standard of care for all patients.
