questionStem: A1/-year-old boy with sickle cell disease is brought to the clinic by his father because of a 4-week history of progressive right hip pain. Initially, the pain was intermittent and the patient rated it as a 5 on a 10-point scale; however, during the past 2 weeks it has become constant, and he now rates the pain as a 9 on a 10-point scale. The pain is not worsened by sneezing, coughing, or lifting objects. He was diagnosed with sickle cell disease at age 3 years; his disease course has been complicated by frequent bouts of dactylitis and pneumonia. He has had two blood transfusions done 9 and 6 years ago, respectively. He has been taking acetaminophen for the hip pain, but it has provided minimal relief. Family history is remarkable for sickle cell disease in his mother, brother, and two sisters, and for sickle cell trait in his father. The patient appears to be in moderate distress. Temperature is 36.6°C (97.8°F), pulse is 98/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 114/68 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a decreased range of motion to hip flexion and abduction. There is no pain on palpation of the lateral aspect of the hip. Muscle strength is 5/5 throughout, and muscle tone is symmetric. Deep tendon reflexes are 1+ in the lower extremities bilaterally. questionStem: A6/-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 24 hours after the onset of double vision, pain behind the right eye, and mild nausea. She describes her double vision as seeing objects side by side. She has hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, peripheral neuropathy, and chronic renal insufficiency. Medications include fosinopril and glyburide. Vital signs are within normal limits. On examination, her double vision is most pronounced when she looks to the right. If she covers either eye, the double vision resolves. The pupils are 3 mm and minimally reactive to light. When the patient looks to the right, the right eye does not abduct. Achilles tendon reflexes are absent. Sensation to pinprick is decreased in a stocking distribution over the feet. An MRI of the brain is most likely to show which of the following?
correctExplanation: The abducens nerve exits the brainstem ventrally at the pontomedullary junction and innervates the lateral rectus muscle of the eye. The most common causes of acute abducens nerve palsy in adults include microvascular ischemia (secondary to diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease), idiopathic causes, and trauma. The abducens nerve is fragile and vulnerable to injury as it crosses the clivus by any mechanism causing downward traction. Abducens nerve palsy presents with binocular horizontal diplopia and ipsilateral abduction deficits of the affected eye. Diagnosis is made on clinical examination, and often there is no definitive finding on MRI. Treatment includes systemic workup for vasculopathic risk factors and patching to reduce diplopia. Abducens nerve palsy secondary to microvascular disease may resolve spontaneously over several months.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. A patient with acute temporal lobe hemorrhage (Choice A) would be more likely to have more pronounced neurologic defects, such as aphasia or hemiparesis. In addition, diplopia that is centrally mediated is typically bilateral, whereas diplopia that resolves when the patient covers one eye is likely due to an ocular cause. Enhancing meninges (Choice B) on MRI would be suggestive of an infectious or inflammatory process such as meningitis. While meningitis can present with focal neurologic deficits, patients typically have other signs or symptoms such as fever and nuchal rigidity. An infarct in the right medulla (Choice C) can lead to lateral medullary syndrome, which can present with ipsilateral ataxia of extremity movements, gait ataxia, Horner syndrome, and can be associated with nystagmus and dysarthria. An orbital tumor (Choice D) would be unlikely to result in abducens nerve palsy. It would more likely directly affect ipsilateral extraocular muscles through local mass effect. Educational Objective: The abducens nerve exits the brainstem ventrally at the pontomedullary junction and innervates the lateral rectus muscle of the eye. Abducens nerve palsy may result from microvascular ischemia and presents with binocular horizontal diplopia and ipsilateral abduction deficits of the affected eye. questionStem: A 32-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 3 hours after the onset of confusion. She appears agitated. She mistakes the attending physician for her brother and insists that he call their father. She admits to drinking regularly since the age of 22 years. Her last drink was 4 ounces of vodka 72 hours ago. Her pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 170/110 mm Hg. Physical examination shows ataxia and a three cycle/sec bilateral hand tremor. On mental status examination, she is oriented to person but not to place or time. After the examination, she yells, "| saw Dad here; why didn't you tell me he was coming to pay my bail? | could be out by now!" Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Alcohol increases the central nervous system activity of y-aminobutyric acid, the main inhibitory neurotransmitter. Abrupt discontinuation of alcohol therefore leads to sympathetic (excitatory) excess. Uncomplicated alcohol withdrawal typically presents with tremors, anxiety, restlessness, headache, nausea, and diaphoresis, which can occur hours after the cessation of alcohol use. If left untreated, alcohol withdrawal can be complicated by seizures and alcoholic hallucinosis (auditory or visual hallucinations). Delirium tremens, the most concerning and life-threatening complication of alcohol withdrawal, typically begins between 48 hours and 1 week after the patient's last drink. Presentation of delirium tremens includes severe confusion and disorientation, fluctuations in consciousness, agitation, visual or auditory hallucinations, and autonomic instability. Alcohol withdrawal is managed supportively with benzodiazepines (eg, lorazepam) to address agitation and prevent or treat the symptoms of withdrawal, along with fluids, nutritional supplementation, and frequent assessment including vital sign monitoring.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Alcoholic hallucinosis (Choice A) is characterized by visual, tactile, or auditory hallucinations beginning 12 to 48 hours after the patient’s last drink. Patients with alcoholic hallucinosis typically have normal vital signs and remain oriented, unlike this patient. Idiosyncratic alcohol intoxication (Choice C) is a type of alcohol-induced psychosis in which ingestion of a small amount of alcohol results in aggression, belligerence, impaired consciousness, and hallucinations. Schizophrenia (Choice D) is a mental disorder characterized by psychosis, disorganized thoughts, and decline in functioning lasting longer than 6 months. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (Choice E) is an irreversible condition caused by vitamin B, (thiamine) deficiency, found most commonly in patients with alcohol use disorder. Patients may present initially with ataxia, confusion, and ophthalmoplegia that progresses to anterograde and retrograde amnesia along with the consequent tendency to confabulate, or verbalize false stories or memories, to compensate for the inability to remember. Educational Objective: Delirium tremens is a life-threatening complication of alcohol withdrawal that presents with confusion, agitation, visual hallucinations, and autonomic instability. questionStem: A24-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 4-month history of generalized weakness and moderate muscle aches. Initially, she had difficulty standing after she removed clothes from the dryer. Now, she has difficulty walking up stairs and rising from a chair. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Her mother has rheumatoid arthritis. Examination of the patient shows periorbital purplish discoloration bilaterally. Cranial nerves are intact. Palpation of all muscles produces pain. Muscle strength is 4/5 in the deltoids, biceps, hip flexors, and quadriceps bilaterally; this result does not change with repeat testing. Muscle bulk and tone are normal. Bilaterally, deep tendon reflexes are 2+ in the brachioradialis muscles and ankles and 1+ in the biceps and quadriceps muscles. Sensation is intact throughout. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Dermatomyositis is an inflammatory condition that affects both skin and musculoskeletal systems. Cutaneous findings of dermatomyositis include a heliotrope rash involving the periocular area, Gottron papules overlying the joints of the dorsal hands, and a poikilodermatous rash distributed over the shoulders and chest/upper torso. Musculoskeletal symptoms include proximal muscle weakness, especially involving the deltoids, biceps, hip flexors, and quadriceps muscles, and patients may report difficulty rising to stand or lifting their arms over the shoulders. Diagnosis is made based on clinical findings and serologic testing, including antinuclear, anti-Jo-1, anti-SRP, and anti-Mi-2 antibodies along with serum creatine kinase assay. Patients diagnosed with dermatomyositis should undergo further workup including age-appropriate cancer screening to rule out an underlying occult malignancy, although malignancy is less common in younger patients.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Charcot-Marie- Tooth disease (Choice A) is a genetic disorder that presents with slowly progressive peripheral neuropathy, often in association with foot deformities such as hammertoes and pes cavus. It is commonly inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. Inclusion body myositis (Choice C) is an idiopathic inflammatory myopathy that commonly affects older males. Symptoms include insidious onset of proximal or distal leg weakness and dysphagia. Characteristic muscle biopsy findings include infiltration of inflammatory cells, fibrosis, and inclusion bodies and/or vacuoles seen with staining. Unlike other inflammatory myopathies, inclusion body myositis is resistant to immunosuppressive therapies. Myasthenia gravis (Choice D) is an autoimmune neuromuscular disorder characterized by the formation of inhibitory antiacetylcholine receptor autoantibodies. Common symptoms include muscular weakness, fatigue, diplopia, and ptosis that worsens toward the end of the day, along with dysphagia and potential respiratory distress. A subset of patients with myasthenia gravis will have a coexisting thymoma. Polymyositis (Choice E) refers to an inflammatory myopathy that presents with proximal muscle pain and weakness. It is an inflammatory myopathy not associated with skin findings that is often treated with immunosuppressive therapy. Educational Objective: Dermatomyositis presents with cutaneous manifestations and proximal muscle weakness. Cutaneous manifestations include pink to light purple patches over the upper eyelids (heliotrope sign), pink papules over the dorsal fingers (Gottron papules), and light pink to lilac patches with telangiectasias over the upper back and sun-exposed chest. questionStem: A 19-year-old man is examined in the intensive care unit 3 days after admission for a self-inflicted gunshot wound to the head. Temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse is 88/min, ventilatory rate is 16/min, and blood pressure is 100/40 mm Hg. Pupils are nonreactive to light. Corneal reflex is absent. Irrigation of the ear canals with cold water results in eye movement only toward the ear being irrigated. On application of noxious stimuli, the patient has only spinal reflex movement. He is not initiating breaths spontaneously above the ventilator. Which of the following findings prevents a diagnosis of brain death in this patient?
correctExplanation: The diagnosis of brain death is determined by the presence of three factors: absence of brainstem reflexes, persistent coma, and lack of spontaneous respirations. Commonly tested brainstem reflexes include the pupillary light response (which tests the optic and oculomotor cranial nerves), the corneal reflex (which tests the trigeminal and facial cranial nerves by lightly touching the cornea with a strand of cotton while observing for blinking or tearing), the pharyngeal and tracheal reflexes (which test the glossopharyngeal and vagus cranial nerves by observing gagging or coughing during endotracheal suctioning), the oculocephalic reflex (which tests the oculomotor, abducens, and vestibulocochlear cranial nerves by assessing for ocular movements during a head turn. Anormal response is eye movement away from the direction of the head turn, whereas an abnormal response is characterized by eye movement with the direction of the head turn, or fixed at midline), and the vestibuloocular reflex. Caloric stimulation, which tests the vestibuloocular reflex, tests the oculomotor, abducens, and vestibulocochlear cranial nerves by assessing for an oculomotor response to irrigation of cold water into one of the ear canals. Cold water irrigation decreases the rate of vestibular afferent signaling within the affected vestibular apparatus, simulating a head turn to the contralateral side. A normal response to cold water irrigation involves tonic deviation toward the ipsilateral ear and horizontal fast nystagmus toward the opposite ear. The fast phase of nystagmus receives input from the dorsal stream of occipitomotor cortex. Absence of fast phase nystagmus suggests an absence of cortical functioning, whereas absence of slow tonic deviation indicates absence of brainstem functioning. Absence of both components of the caloric test is required for the diagnosis of brain death. This patient's caloric testing, which demonstrates slow tonic deviation toward the side of cold water irrigation, may prevent a diagnosis of brain death.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. The corneal reflex (Choice B) tests the trigeminal and facial cranial nerves by lightly touching the cornea with a strand of cotton while observing for blinking or tearing. This patient's corneal reflex is absent, which could be consistent with a diagnosis of brain death. The pupillary light reflex (Choice C) tests the optic and oculomotor cranial nerves by assessing for pupillary constriction in response to light. This patient lacks a pupillary light response, which could be consistent with a diagnosis of brain death. Motor response (Choice D) testing assesses for a motor response to painful or noxious stimuli. The presence of spinal reflex movement in this patient does not indicate an intact motor response. Respiratory effort (Choice E) is assessed with apnea testing by withdrawing the patient from ventilator support. This is typically the final step in diagnosis of brain death. While this patient does not yet have a positive apnea test, lack of spontaneous breaths above the ventilator is consistent with a diagnosis of brain death. questionStem: A4-year-old boy is brought to the physician because he walks predominately on his toes. He was born at 29 weeks' gestation and has a history of hyaline membrane disease and a grade | intraventricular hemorrhage. He takes albuterol for asthma, and his immunizations are up-to-date. He sat up at the age of 9 months and walked at 18 months; he currently uses full sentences when talking. He is at the 50th percentile for both height and weight. Examination shows generalized hyperreflexia, a persistent Babinski sign bilaterally, heel cord contractures, and decreased abduction and external rotation of the hips. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Cerebral palsy is a disorder of nonprogressive central motor dysfunction as a result of impaired fetal or neonatal brain development. The cause is frequently multifactorial, though the most important factors are premature delivery, which may increase the risk for cerebral palsy 80-fold, and low birth weight. Patients who are born prematurely may have also experienced other sequelae of prematurity, including hyaline membrane disease, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, intraventricular hemorrhage, necrotizing enterocolitis, and retinopathy of prematurity. Other risk factors include intrauterine infections, antepartum hemorrhage, placental pathology, multiple pregnancy, heavy maternal alcohol use, maternal smoking, and maternal obesity, though for many of these factors, causality has not been established. During this period, she has had difficulty climbing one flight of stairs and combing her hair. She also reports double vision that occurs when she reads. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows bilateral ptosis. Muscle strength is 4/5 in all extremities. questionStem: A37/-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of joint pain. The symptoms initially began with increasing pain in his left knee and have progressed to include his right Knee and left hip. There is no history of trauma. Six weeks ago, he had fever, malaise, and a 5-cm rash with central clearing on his chest that resolved spontaneously after 7 days. Examination of the left knee shows no warmth or erythema. Range of motion of the left knee is full and does not produce pain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Lyme arthritis, one of several complications of Lyme disease, is caused by disseminated Borrelia burgdorferi infection. B. burgdorferi are transmitted following tick bites, most commonly from Ixodes ticks. Initial manifestations of Lyme disease include the erythema chronicum migrans rash, which is an expanding rash with a central ring-like clearing and targetoid appearance. It generally appears within 1 to 2 weeks of the tick bite. Left untreated, a subset of patients will develop disseminated disease that may result in Bell palsy, meningitis, myopericarditis, or arthritis. Patients may be diagnosed clinically when the characteristic erythema migrans rash is observed in the setting of known or probable recent exposure to a tick in an endemic area. Serologic testing is controversial as it may show false positives or negatives; however, it may be used to support the diagnosis in later stage disease. Patients with Lyme disease are treated with doxycycline or amoxicillin. Most patients with Lyme arthritis will demonstrate response to therapy.

He has used a wheelchair since an accidental gunshot transected his spine at the T9 level 20 years ago. On arrival, he is too confused to provide his medical history. correctExplanation: Delirium is defined by an acute-onset alteration of consciousness and cognition, with symptoms that wax and wane throughout the day. In elderly patients, especially those with underlying dementia, systemic infection can rapidly lead to the development of delirium. Other common causes of delirium include intoxication and adverse effects from medications such as anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, or opiates. All patients with delirium should be evaluated for evidence of systemic infection with urinalysis and culture, chest x-ray, and occasionally with blood cultures, if indicated. Treatment of delirium should focus on treatment of the underlying infection if one is detected, frequent reorientation, maintenance of normal sleep-wake cycles, and placement of the patient in a calm and soothing environment. She has not had fever, nausea, vomiting, or weakness. She has a 5-year history of AIDS currently treated with three-drug antiretroviral therapy. There is no papilledema. Examination of the oropharynx shows thrush. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. Her CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 25/mm3 (Normal2500), and plasma HIV viral load is 5000 copies/mL. A CT scan of the head with contrast shows five 1- to 2-cm, ring-enhancing lesions. Cerebral toxoplasmosis is an AIDS- defining disease caused by Toxoplasma gondii and is the most common cause of multiple ring-enhancing lesions on CT scan of the head in a patient with AIDS. Transmission can occur through the ingestion of oocysts from soil contaminated with cat feces or infected meat, direct transmission between a mother and fetus, or from organ transplantation, which leads to invasion followed by dissemination of the parasite where it typically lies dormant. It is a ubiquitous organism, and nearly 10% of individuals will be seropositive for T. gondii, but the parasite does not usually cause severe disease in immunocompetent individuals. In patients with HIV infection and CD4+ counts less than 100 cells/mm?, however, reactivation can occur with several distinct clinical syndromes of which cerebral toxoplasmosis results in the most morbidity. Cerebral toxoplasmosis typically presents with multiple ring-enhancing lesions scattered throughout the brain. Seizures, focal neurologic deficits, and systemic symptoms are common, as are signs of increased intracranial pressure. Patients with HIV and positive Toxoplasma |gG antibodies are typically treated empirically with a sulfonamide and pyrimethamine if cerebral toxoplasmosis is suspected, but confirmatory diagnosis occurs through a brain biopsy, which will show a dense infiltrate of lymphocytes, macrophages, and plasma cells, along with the presence of the 7. gondii organism.

questionStem: A 32-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of low back pain that began 4 hours after he lifted a sofa. His symptoms have gradually become worse, and he now has severe pain with any movement of his back. The pain radiates to the right posterior thigh. He has had no changes in bowel or bladder function. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg. On examination, flexion and extension of the waist and twisting movements of the torso increase the pain. There is tenderness over the lumbar paraspinous musculature bilaterally that is more prominent on the right. Straight-leg raising on the right causes pain in the right sacral area at 45 degrees. Neurologic examination shows no other abnormalities. Sensation is intact. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?

choices.E: Nerve conduction studies of the lower extremities

correctExplanation: This patient's presentation is suggestive of acute onset of low back pain, which lasts up to 4 weeks and may be attributed to musculoskeletal injury from exertion, overuse, or trauma. Symptoms include pain with movement and paraspinal tenderness in the absence of neurologic symptoms or bony tenderness. Most cases resolve with conservative management, which includes activity modification, stretching and physical therapy, over-the-counter analgesics such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, massage, and heat therapy. Certain red flag signs and symptoms should prompt more urgent evaluation for an alternate cause, especially if there is concern for infection, malignancy, spinal cord compromise, or vertebral fracture. These include but are not limited to new fevers, intravenous drug use, focal neurologic deficits (eg, urinary retention, saddle anesthesia, bowel incontinence which may suggest cauda equina syndrome), progressive lower extremity neurologic symptoms, current or recent cancer history, advanced age, systemic corticosteroid use, and a significant traumatic mechanism. In this young, otherwise healthy patient with a mild inciting event, the most appropriate initial step in management is ibuprofen therapy.

Activity modification for symptom relief should be advised, with encouragement to continue normal activities of daily living and non-exacerbating exertion. X-rays of the lumbosacral spine (Choice B) and MRI of the lumbosacral spine (Choice C) should be reserved for patients who present with red flag signs and symptoms to evaluate for evidence of infection, malignancy, spinal cord compromise, or vertebral fracture. For otherwise healthy patients with back pain that has persisted for a subacute time course, imaging studies do not generally change management. Nerve conduction studies of the lower extremities (Choice E), including electromyography, should be reserved for patients who experience neurologic symptoms including weakness or altered sensation.
